| **Palpitations** | हृदय की तेज धड़कन / दिल बैठना | Rapid, strong, or irregular heartbeats due to agitation |
| **Pettifogger** | क्षुद्र या चालाक वकील / धूर्त झगड़ालू | An unscrupulous lawyer or someone engaged in petty quibbles |
| **Dessiatin** | डेसियाटिन (रूसी भूमि माप: ~2.7 एकड़) | An old Russian measure of land equal to approximately 2.7 acres |
| **Perpetuity** | शाश्वत काल / हमेशा के लिए | The state or quality of lasting forever or indefinitely |
| **Birchwoods** | भोजपत्र के पेड़ों का जंगल | Woods or groves composed of birch trees |
| **Overshot** | ऊपरी जबड़ा निचले जबड़े से आगे निकला हुआ | In the play, Lomov says Squeezer's lower jaw is shorter than the upper jaw. |
| **Spasms** | ऐंठन / झटके | Sudden involuntary muscle contractions or twitches |
| **Lovesick cat** | प्रेम की दीवानी बिल्ली | Someone foolishly yearning for romantic attention |
| **Stuffed sausage** | भरवां कबाब (मोटा मूर्ख व्यक्ति) | A contemptuous Russian insult for a pompous, foolish man |
| **Wizen-faced frump** | झुर्रियों वाले चेहरे वाला फुहड़ व्यक्ति | A withered, untidy, and unattractive person |

---
💡 10. Answer-writing and exam presentation practice

### ✍️ Topper's Golden Rules for 'The Proposal':
1. **Always Mention Dramatic Genre:** Identify the play as a *one-act farce* by *Anton Chekhov*, satirizing the *19th-century Russian landed aristocracy*.
2. **Highlight the Contrast between Formality and Vulgarity:**
   - Contrast Lomov's *evening dress and gloves* with the vulgar name-calling (*"pettifogger", "stuffed sausage", "malicious rogue"*).
3. **Memorize Key Numerical Data for Objective/Short Answers:**
   - Lomov (35 years), Natalya (25 years).
   - Oxen Meadows: 5 dessiatins, 300 roubles.
   - Guess (125 roubles), Squeezer (85 roubles).
4. **End Long Answers with Chekhov's Social Critique:**
   - Emphasize that marriage is shown as an economic alliance between land-owners rather than an emotional union of hearts.

### 🌟 Hindi Comprehensive Explanation Summary (हिंदी सारांश एवं परीक्षा सार)
'द प्रपोजल' (विवाह का प्रस्ताव) महान रूसी नाटककार एवं कथाकार एंटोन चेखव द्वारा रचित एक हास्य-प्रधान एकांकी प्रहसन (Farce) है। यह नाटक 19वीं सदी के अंत में रूसी जमींदार वर्ग की संकीर्ण मानसिकता, झूठे दंभ और विवाह को केवल एक आर्थिक सौदे के रूप में देखने की प्रवृत्ति पर करारा व्यंग्य करता है।

इवान वासिलीविच लोमोव (35 वर्ष) एक रोगभ्रमी (Hypochondriac) और अविवाहित जमींदार है, जो अपने पड़ोसी स्टीफन स्टीपानोविच चुबुकोव की 25 वर्षीय बेटी नताल्या से विवाह का प्रस्ताव लेकर आता है। वह शाम की औपचारिक पोशाक (टेलकोट और दस्ताने) में सज-धज कर पहुँचता है। चुबुकोव पहले सोचता है कि वह पैसे उधार माँगने आया है, परंतु जब उसे विवाह के प्रस्ताव की बात पता चलती है, तो वह खुशी से रो पड़ता है और नताल्या को बुलाने जाता है जिसे वह 'प्रेम की भूखी बिल्ली' कहता है।

लोमोव का विवाह का निर्णय किसी प्रेम पर नहीं बल्कि व्यावहारिक गणना पर आधारित है—वह 35 वर्ष का हो चुका है, उसे दिल की धड़कन (palpitations) और अनिद्रा की बीमारी है और वह एक नियमित जीवन जीना चाहता है। नताल्या घर के काम-काज में कुशल और पढ़ी-लिखी है।

परंतु जब नताल्या आती है, तो बातचीत के दौरान लोमोव अनजाने में 'ऑक्सेन मीडोज़' (बैलों की चरागाह) का उल्लेख 'मेरी जमीन' कहकर कर देता है। इस पर दोनों में भयानक विवाद छिड़ जाता है। नताल्या कहती है कि वह जमीन उनकी है, जबकि लोमोव अपनी बुआ की दादी और चुबुकोव के दादा के किसानों का ऐतिहासिक हवाला देता है। केवल 300 रूबल और 5 डेसियाटिन जमीन के लिए दोनों एक-दूसरे पर चीखने लगते हैं। चुबुकोव भी विवाद में कूद पड़ता है और दोनों पक्ष एक-दूसरे के खानदान को गालियाँ देने लगते हैं। दिल की धड़कन बढ़ने पर लोमोव घर से बाहर भाग जाता है।

लोमोव के जाने के बाद जब चुबुकोव बताता है कि वह तो विवाह का प्रस्ताव लेकर आया था, तो नताल्या सिर पीट लेती है और चीखने-चिल्लाने लगती है—"उसे वापस लाओ!" चुबुकोव दुखी होकर कहता है कि जवान बेटी का बाप होना कितना बड़ा सिरदर्द है।

लोमोव लंगड़ाते हुए लौटता है। नताल्या जमीन विवाद को सुलझाकर बात संभालती है, परंतु तभी शिकार के कुत्तों पर दूसरा घमासान छिड़ जाता है। लोमोव अपने 125 रूबल के कुत्ते 'गैस' (Guess) को श्रेष्ठ बताता है, जबकि नताल्या अपने 85 रूबल के कुत्ते 'स्क्वीज़र' (Squeezer) को। चिल्लाते-चिल्लाते लोमोव अचेत होकर गिर पड़ता है। नताल्या सोचती है कि वह मर गया है और रोने लगती है। जब लोमोव को होश आता है, तो चुबुकोव बिना देर किए नताल्या का हाथ लोमोव के हाथ में थमाकर कहता है—"जल्दी से ब्याह करो और जान छोड़ो!" दोनों एक-दूसरे को चूमते हैं, परंतु अगले ही पल फिर बहस शुरू हो जाती है कि 'गैस' बेहतर है या 'स्क्वीज़र'। चुबुकोव शैम्पेन का गिलास उठाते हुए कहता है—"चलो, बला टली!" नाटक हास्य और व्यंग्य के साथ समाप्त होता है।

---

### 🎯 10-Mark Self-Assessment Challenge (Time: 15 Minutes)

1. What was the age of Lomov and Natalya? (1 Mark)
2. What did Chubukov initially suspect Lomov had come for? (1 Mark)
3. Name the two subjects over which Lomov and Natalya fought. (2 Marks)
4. Why did Chubukov call a grown-up daughter a 'burden'? (2 Marks)
5. Explain how 'The Proposal' ridicules the materialistic nature of upper-class marriages. (4 Marks)

#### 📝 Scoring Key & Hints:
- **Q1:** Lomov was 35 years old; Natalya was 25 years old.
- **Q2:** To borrow money.
- **Q3:** 1. The ownership of Oxen Meadows; 2. The superiority of their hunting dogs (Guess vs. Squeezer).
- **Q4:** Because managing her emotional hysterics, marriage prospects, and unending arguments caused him unbearable stress.
- **Q5:** Neither Lomov nor Natalya loves each other romantically; their union is based on expanding estates and social vanity. Even during their betrothal, their material greed and petty ego take precedence over genuine affection.

**Syllabus source correction, 13 October 2026:** Scope/marks above use the [Madhyamik Class 10 syllabus, PDF pp. 3–5](https://rajeduboard.rajasthan.gov.in/anudeshika-etc/10_2027.pdf), not the separate Praveshika scheme. This correction does not certify the remaining exercise keys.

chapters.title: RBSE Class 10 English: First Flight Poetry, Poem 1

content.value: “Dust of Snow” — Robert Frost

माध्यमिक शिक्षा बोर्ड राजस्थान (कक्षा 10 अंग्रेजी - प्रथम उड़ान: पद्य खंड)

---

> **Syllabus note:** RBSE 2026–27 assigns 40 marks to Literature across First Flight and Footprints Without Feet; it does not state poem-specific weights or guaranteed question formats. The following poem analysis is for practice and revision.

---
⚡ 1. 10-Second Mind Map & Core Philosophy

### 1.1 Visual Architectural Mind Map ``` ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ DUST OF SNOW (Robert Frost) │ └────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┘ │ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ ┌─────────────────────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────────────────────┐ │ THE NATURAL IMAGES │ │ THE POEM'S EVENT │ │ THE SPEAKER'S RESPONSE │ │ • A crow │ │ • Snow falls from a hemlock tree│ │ • "A change of mood" │ │ • A hemlock tree │ ──► │ • "Shook down on me" │ ──► │ • "Saved some part" │ │ • Snow │ │ • No physical sensation specified│ │ • Part of a regretted day saved│ └─────────────────────────────────┘ └─────────────────────────────────┘ └─────────────────────────────────┘ │ │ │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────┘ ▼ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ CENTRAL IDEA │ │ A small event in nature changes the speaker's mood and │ │ saves part of a day he had regretted. │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ ``` --- ### 1.2 Core Philosophy & Deep Philosophical Underpinnings * **Contrast in the poem's natural images (प्राकृतिक बिंबों का विरोध):** The poem pairs a crow and a hemlock tree with a change of mood. It does not explain the poet's choice or establish universal meanings for these images. A hemlock tree is a conifer in genus *Tsuga*; it is distinct from poison hemlock (*Conium maculatum*), the plant associated with the traditional account of Socrates' death. A poison association may be offered as an interpretation, not as the tree's botanical identity or a stated fact of the poem. * **A small event and a change of mood (छोटी घटना और मनोदशा में परिवर्तन):** The speaker says that snow shaken down by a crow changed his mood and saved part of a day he had regretted. The poem does not name a clinical state, explain the source or duration of the regret, or claim that the change was a psychological treatment. * **What the poem leaves unstated (कविता में अनकही बातें):** The poem does not say that snow landed on bare skin, describe a cold shock, or connect the event with a modern grounding exercise. Those may be creative classroom comparisons, but they should not be presented as facts about the poem or clinical equivalences. * **Part of the day is saved (दिन का कुछ हिस्सा बचना):** The speaker says that “some part” of a day he had rued was saved. The poem does not say it was morning, how much time had passed, or what he did afterward. A reader may take the line as a hopeful turn, while keeping that interpretation distinct from the stated event. --- ### 1.3 Biographical & Literary Context: Robert Frost (1874–1963) * **Robert Frost:** Robert Frost (1874–1963) was an American poet and received four Pulitzer Prizes for Poetry. Avoid reducing British Romantic poets to a claim that they escaped into utopian daydreams; that is an opinion, not a verifiable fact about this poem. * **Style:** Frost is known for poems using colloquial speech and rural settings. * **Publication History:** 'Dust of Snow' was originally published in 1923 in Frost’s landmark collection *New Hampshire*, which earned him his first Pulitzer Prize in 1924. --- ### 1.4 Structural & Metrical Anatomy Matrix | Structural Parameter | Technical Specification | Functional Poetic Purpose | |:---|:---|:---| | **Form & Stanzaic Division** | Two quatrains (2 stanzas of 4 lines each = 8 lines total) | The first stanza describes the event; the second reports the speaker's response. | | **Meter** | No fixed meter label is assigned in this guide. | Avoid presenting a disputed scansion as settled fact. | | **Syllable Count** | No fixed syllable-count rule is claimed. | Count depends on pronunciation. | | **Rhyme Scheme** | Stanza 1: **a-b-a-b** (`crow` / `me` / `snow` / `tree`)
Stanza 2: **c-d-c-d** (`heart` / `mood` / `part` / `rued`) | Alternating rhyme binds the stanzas melodically, maintaining brisk narrative pace. | | **Syntactic Construction** | One sentence across all 8 lines, ending with a period. | Any effect attributed to that structure is an interpretation. | ---
2. Poetic features

The examples below are text-based observations. Effects and symbolic meanings may be interpreted differently by readers.

```
TEXT-BASED OBSERVATIONS
• End rhyme in both stanzas
• Repetition of the initial /s/ sound in “saved some”
• Syntax continues across line breaks
• Natural images followed by a reported change of mood
```

### 2.1 Textual features

| Feature | Textual basis | Note |
|:---|:---|:---|
| End rhyme | *crow/snow*, *me/tree*, *heart/part*, *mood/rued* | The rhyme scheme is *abab cdcd*. |
| Alliteration | *saved some* | The initial /s/ sound is repeated. |
| Line breaks | The syntax continues across several line breaks. | This can be discussed as enjambment; its effect is open to interpretation. |
| Figurative language | *heart* in “Has given my heart / A change of mood” | It may be read figuratively as the seat of feeling. More specific labels should be supported. |
| Imagery | A crow, a hemlock tree, and snow | The text does not specify the bird's color, a dark bark, a location, or a physical sensation. |

---
3. Stanza-by-stanza text, vocabulary, Hindi paraphrase, and practice questions

### 📖 Stanza 1 (Lines 1–4)

```
"The way a crow
Shook down on me
The dust of snow
From a hemlock tree"
```

#### 📘 Word Meanings & Grammatical Glossary
* **The way (adverbial phrase):** The specific manner, motion, or sudden gesture (जिस प्रकार / जिस ढंग से).
* **Crow (noun):** A crow; the poem does not identify its species or assign it a universal symbolic meaning (कौआ; कविता में प्रजाति नहीं बताई गई है).
* **Shook down (phrasal verb - past tense of 'shake down'):** Dislodged, caused to fall by vibrating or disturbing the branch (झकझोर कर नीचे गिरा दिया).
* **Dust of snow (noun phrase):** Fine snow shaken from the tree (बर्फ के महीन कण).
* **Hemlock tree (noun):** A conifer in the genus *Tsuga*. It is botanically distinct from poison hemlock (*Conium maculatum*), a flowering herb. The poem does not identify the tree to species.

#### 🇮🇳 Hindi Paraphrase & Deep Philosophical Commentary (विस्तृत भावार्थ)
कवि बताता है कि एक कौवे ने हेमलॉक वृक्ष से बर्फ के महीन कण उसके ऊपर गिरा दिए। इस छोटी-सी घटना से उसका मन बदल गया और उस दिन का कुछ हिस्सा बच गया, जिसे वह पहले पछतावे से देख रहा था। कविता उसके पछतावे का कारण, कौवे की हरकत का तरीका, या बर्फ गिरने की शारीरिक अनुभूति नहीं बताती।

कौवे और हेमलॉक वृक्ष को कुछ पाठक परंपरागत रूप से अशुभ या उदास छवियों के रूप में पढ़ सकते हैं; यह एक साहित्यिक व्याख्या है। हेमलॉक वृक्ष को विषैली जड़ी-बूटी poison hemlock (*Conium maculatum*) समझना वनस्पति-विज्ञान की दृष्टि से गलत होगा। कविता का मुख्य स्पष्ट परिवर्तन यह है कि प्रकृति की एक छोटी घटना वक्ता की मनोदशा बदलती है।

---

#### 📝 Stanza comprehension practice (suggested format, not an official RBSE pattern)

**Q1. Where was the poet standing or walking, and what unexpected incident occurred? (कवि कहाँ खड़ा था और क्या अप्रत्याशित घटना घटी?)**  
*Model Answer:* A crow shook some snow from a hemlock tree onto the speaker. The poem does not say where exactly the speaker was standing or how the crow moved. *(1 suggested mark)*

**Q2. What change does the speaker say the incident brought about? (वक्ता के अनुसार इस घटना से क्या परिवर्तन आया?)**
*Model Answer:* The speaker says the incident changed his mood and saved part of a day he had regretted. *(1 suggested mark)*

**Q3. Identify the rhyme scheme and the rhyming words of this stanza. (इस पद्यांश की तुकबंदी योजना और तुक वाले शब्द लिखिए।)**  
*Model Answer:* The rhyme scheme is **a-b-a-b**. The rhyming word pairs are: **crow – snow** and **me – tree**. *(1 suggested mark)*

**Q4. Find a word from the stanza which means 'powdery particles' and state its grammatical part of speech. (पद्यांश से 'बारीक कण' अर्थ वाला शब्द खोजिए तथा उसका शब्द-भेद बताइए।)**  
*Model Answer:* The word is **'dust'** (in *dust of snow*), functioning here as a **noun**. *(1 suggested mark)*

---

### 📖 Stanza 2 (Lines 5–8)

```
"Has given my heart
A change of mood
And saved some part
Of a day I had rued."
```

#### 📘 Word Meanings & Grammatical Glossary
* **Given (verb - past participle of 'give'):** Bestowed, imparted, granted (प्रदान किया / भर दिया).
* **Heart (noun):** Used figuratively in the phrase “change of mood”; a definite synecdoche label is interpretive (हृदय / मनोभाव).
* **Change of mood (noun phrase):** A change in the speaker's mood; the poem does not specify every feeling before and after it (मनोदशा में परिवर्तन).
* **Saved (verb - past tense):** Preserved or rescued from being lost (बचा लिया).
* **Part (noun):** A fragment, portion, or the remainder of the day (दिन का शेष भाग).
* **Rued (verb - past participle of 'rue'):** Felt bitter regret, remorse, sorrow, or lamented over wasted time (पछतावे में बिताना / शोक में व्यर्थ गंवाना).

#### 🇮🇳 Hindi Paraphrase & Deep Philosophical Commentary (विस्तृत भावार्थ)
वक्ता कहता है कि बर्फ के कण गिरने की घटना से उसके मन का भाव बदल गया और उस दिन का कुछ हिस्सा बच गया, जिसे वह पहले पछतावे से देख रहा था। कविता इस परिवर्तन को बताती है, पर उसके कारण, शारीरिक अनुभूति, या बाद के कामों का विवरण नहीं देती। पाठक इसे छोटे प्राकृतिक अनुभव के सकारात्मक प्रभाव के रूप में समझ सकते हैं।

---

#### 📝 Stanza comprehension practice (suggested format, not official RBSE pattern)

**Q1. What change in mood does the speaker report in Stanza 2? (द्वितीय पद्यांश में वक्ता अपनी मनोदशा में क्या परिवर्तन बताता है?)**  
*Model Answer:* His mood changed. The poem presents this as positive because he says the event saved part of a day he had rued; it does not list a clinical or detailed emotional state. *(1 suggested mark)*

**Q2. What does the poet mean by the expression "a day I had rued"? (अभिव्यक्ति 'a day I had rued' से कवि का क्या अभिप्राय है?)**  
*Model Answer:* “Rued” means regretted. The wording does not tell us the cause of the regret or how much of the day had passed. *(1 suggested mark)*

**Q3. Name the poetic device utilized in the line "And saved some part". Cite the specific phonetic sound. (पंक्ति "And saved some part" में प्रयुक्त काव्य उपकरण और विशिष्ट ध्वनि बताइए।)**  
*Model Answer:* The poetic device is **Alliteration**, marked by the melodious repetition of the initial consonant sound **/s/** in the words *saved* and *some*. *(1 suggested mark)*

**Q4. What does “rued” mean? ("rued" का क्या अर्थ है?)**  
*Model Answer:* It means regretted. *(1 suggested mark)*

---
4. Text-based model answers

**Central idea (30–40 words):** A crow shakes snow from a hemlock tree onto the speaker. This small event changes his mood and saves part of a day he had regretted. The poem leaves the cause of his regret unexplained.

**Meaning of “a day I had rued”:** The speaker says he had regretted the day. The text does not specify why he felt this way or how much of the day had passed.

**Effect of the incident:** The speaker reports a change in mood and says that some part of his day was saved. More detailed feelings such as clinical depression, physical shock, or a guaranteed return to happiness go beyond the poem.

**Images and interpretation:** A reader may interpret the crow or hemlock tree symbolically, but those meanings should be labelled as interpretation. A hemlock tree is not poison hemlock.

---
5. Accuracy notes for students

| Point | Reliable answer guidance |
|:---|:---|
| What the poem states | A crow shakes snow from a hemlock tree; the speaker reports a change of mood and that part of a regretted day was saved. |
| What “rued” means | Regretted. The poem does not identify the reason for the regret. |
| Hemlock | A hemlock tree is a conifer in genus *Tsuga*. Poison hemlock (*Conium maculatum*) is a different plant. |
| Rhyme and sound | End rhymes include *crow/snow*, *me/tree*, *heart/part*, and *mood/rued*. “Saved some” repeats the initial /s/ sound. |
| Interpretation | Symbolism, irony, or the emotional effect of the images can be discussed, but should be presented as a supported reading rather than as a stated fact. |
6. Practice question bank

These questions are for revision. Their provenance as RBSE past-paper questions has not been established; mark values are suggested only.

1. **What is “dust of snow,” and what effect does it have on the speaker?** *(Suggested: 2 marks)*  
   It refers to snow shaken down by a crow from a hemlock tree. The speaker says the event changed his mood and saved part of a day he had rued.

2. **What does “rued” mean?** *(Suggested: 1 mark)*  
   It means regretted. The poem does not say what caused the speaker's regret.

3. **What are the rhyme scheme and rhyming pairs in stanza one?** *(Suggested: 2 marks)*  
   The rhyme scheme is *abab*: *crow/snow* and *me/tree*.

4. **How might the crow and hemlock tree contribute to the poem's effect?** *(Suggested: 2 marks)*  
   A reader may interpret the natural images as unexpected agents of change. The poem states that the crow shakes snow from the tree and that the speaker's mood changes; further symbolism should be identified as interpretation.

5. **Identify an example of alliteration.** *(Suggested: 1 mark)*  
   “Saved some” repeats the initial /s/ sound.

---
7. Practice questions (suggested format, not official RBSE pattern)

### Practice stanza 1 (suggested one mark per question)
```
The way a crow
Shook down on me
The dust of snow
From a hemlock tree
```
1. Name the poem and the poet. *(1 suggested mark)*
2. What fell on the poet and from where? *(1 suggested mark)*
3. What tree is named in the stanza? *(1 suggested mark)*
4. Identify the rhyming pair for the word 'crow'. *(1 suggested mark)*

### Practice stanza 2 (suggested one mark per question)
```
Has given my heart
A change of mood
And saved some part
Of a day I had rued.
```
1. What gave the poet's heart a change of mood? *(1 suggested mark)*
2. What does “rued” mean? *(1 suggested mark)*
3. Name two words in this stanza that begin with the same consonant sound. *(1 suggested mark)*
4. What does “rued” mean? *(1 suggested mark)*

---

### ✍️ Short Answer Practice Questions (20–30 Words each - 2 Marks)
1. What was the physical action of the crow that affected the poet?
2. How does the poem demonstrate that human beings can find solace in unexpected places?
3. What effect does the snow incident have on the speaker, according to the poem?
4. What change does the speaker report after the snow falls?
5. The poem is one sentence across eight lines. What effect might this structure create?

---

### 📖 Long Answer Practice Questions (60–80 Words - 4 Marks)
1. **Critical Appreciation:** Write a comprehensive critical appreciation of Robert Frost's poem 'Dust of Snow', highlighting its themes, tone, imagery, and poetic craftsmanship.
2. **Comparative Essay:** Compare the presentation of nature in 'Dust of Snow' with traditional Romantic nature poetry. How does Frost establish modern realism?

---
8. Rapid revision and self-assessment practice

### 🚀 Rapid Revision Cheat Sheet

| Parameter | Quick Memory Anchor |
|:---|:---|
| **Poet & Nationality** | Robert Frost — American Poet of Rural Realism (1874–1963) |
| **Structure & Meter** | 8 lines, 2 quatrains, one sentence; short rhythmic lines (avoid a fixed meter claim) |
| **Rhyme Scheme** | Stanza 1: **abab** \| Stanza 2: **cdcd** |
| **Central Images** | Crow, hemlock tree, falling snow, and a change of mood; symbolic meanings are interpretations |
| **Poetic Devices** | Line breaks and end rhymes; *saved some* repeats an initial /s/ sound. Interpret other devices with care. |
| **Central idea** | A brief encounter with nature changes the speaker’s mood and saves part of a day he had regretted. |

---

### Self-assessment test (suggested 10 marks, 15 minutes)

**Section A: Objective & Vocabulary (3 Marks)**
1. Which statement distinguishes a hemlock tree from poison hemlock?  
   (a) A fragrant flowering bush  
   (b) A conifer; distinct from poison hemlock, which is a flowering herb  
   (c) A sweet fruit tree  
   (d) A medicinal pine  
2. What does the word 'rued' mean in the poem?  
   (a) Ruled like a king  
   (b) Regretted bitterly  
   (c) Celebrated gladly  
   (d) Planned carefully  
3. The rhyme scheme of the poem is:  
   (a) aabb ccdd  
   (b) abba cddc  
   (c) abab cdcd  
   (d) abcd abcd  

**Section B: Stanza comprehension practice (4 suggested marks)**
Read the stanza and answer:
> *"The way a crow / Shook down on me / The dust of snow / From a hemlock tree"*  
4. Name the bird and the tree mentioned in the extract. *(1 suggested mark)*  
5. What physical object fell upon the poet? *(1 suggested mark)*  
6. Name the literary device used when a sentence runs into the next line without punctuation. *(1 suggested mark)*  
7. Write the rhyming word for 'tree'. *(1 suggested mark)*  

**Section C: Short answer practice (3 suggested marks)**
8. Explain how the falling of the dust of snow saved some part of the poet's day. (Answer in 30 words) *(3 suggested marks)*

---

### Suggested answer key (not an official marking scheme)

* **1.** (b) A conifer; distinct from poison hemlock, a flowering herb. *(1 suggested mark)*
* **2.** (b) Regretted bitterly *(1 suggested mark)*
* **3.** (c) abab cdcd *(1 suggested mark)*
* **4.** Bird: The crow; Tree: The hemlock tree. *(1 suggested mark)*
* **5.** Fine, powdery particles of snow ("dust of snow"). *(1 suggested mark)*
* **6.** Enjambment. *(1 suggested mark)*
* **7.** me. *(1 suggested mark)*
* **8. Suggested answer:**  
  * The speaker says a crow shook snow from a hemlock tree onto him. *(suggested point)*  
  * He says the incident changed his mood. *(suggested point)*  
  * He says it saved part of a day he had rued. The text does not detail the rest of the day. *(suggested point)*

content.value: “Fire and Ice” — Robert Frost

माध्यमिक शिक्षा बोर्ड राजस्थान (कक्षा 10 अंग्रेजी - प्रथम उड़ान: पद्य खंड)

---

> **Syllabus note:** RBSE 2026–27 assigns 40 marks to Literature across First Flight and Footprints Without Feet; it does not state poem-specific weights or guaranteed question formats. The following poem analysis is for practice and revision.

---
⚡ 1. 10-Second Mind Map & Core Philosophy

### 1.1 Visual Architectural Mind Map

```
                          ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
                          │                FIRE AND ICE (Robert Frost)              │
                          └────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┘
                                                       │
         ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         ▼                                             ▼                                             ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────┐       ┌─────────────────────────────────┐       ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│ FIRE (अग्नि)                    │       │       THE SPEAKER'S REASON      │       │ ICE (बर्फ)                      │
│ • Linked with desire             │       │ • “Some say” introduces views   │       │ • Linked with hate              │
│ • Speaker favors fire            │  ──►  │ • The world “perish twice”      │  ──►  │ • Ice could also suffice        │
│ • “tasted of desire”             │       │ • A hypothetical second end     │       │ • “I think I know enough”       │
└─────────────────────────────────┘       └─────────────────────────────────┘       └─────────────────────────────────┘
         │                                             │                                             │
         └─────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                                       ▼
                          ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
                          │                    CORE PHILOSOPHY                      │
                          │ The speaker links fire with desire and ice with hate.   │
                          │ He favors fire, but says ice would also suffice if the  │
                          │ world had to perish twice.                              │
                          └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

### 1.2 Reading the poem

The speaker presents fire and ice as possible ends for the world, then links fire with “desire” and ice with “hate.” Readers often extend these images to other forms of desire, greed, or hostility, but those are interpretations rather than an exhaustive list in the poem. The final claim that ice “would suffice” supports a reading that the two forces are both capable of destruction; the poem does not compare them with a scientific measure.

The poem's restrained wording, repeated sounds, and movement from fire to ice can support discussion of tone and contrast. Statements that desire is fast or irrational, or that hatred is slow and calculating, go beyond what the text says.

### 1.3 Context and publication

* **Harlow Shapley anecdote:** Harvard astronomer Harlow Shapley later recalled a conversation in which Frost asked how the world might end. Shapley said he described possible destruction by solar heat or by freezing. Treat this as Shapley's retrospective account, not verified proof that the exchange was the poem's sole inspiration.
* **Publication:** The poem appeared in *Harper's Magazine* in December 1920 and was collected in *New Hampshire* (1923). The collection received the 1924 Pulitzer Prize for Poetry.
### 1.4 Structural & Metrical Anatomy Matrix

| Structural Parameter | Technical Specification | Functional Poetic Purpose |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Form** | One stanza of 9 lines. | The poem presents a compact argument. |
| **Meter** | Often scanned as a mix of iambic tetrameter and dimeter; individual readings may vary. | Treat scansion as analysis, not a syllabus fact. |
| **Rhyme Scheme** | **ABAAB CBCB** | The end-rhyme groups are *fire/desire*, *ice/twice/suffice*, and *hate/great*. |
| **Tone** | The wording is conversational; readers may describe it as understated or ironic. | Tone labels are interpretive. |

---
2. Poetic features

| Feature | Textual basis | Note |
|:---|:---|:---|
| End rhyme | *fire/desire/fire*, *ice/twice/ice/suffice*, *hate/great* | The pattern is *ABAAB CBCB*. |
| Repetition | “Some say” begins lines 1 and 2. | This is repetition at the start of consecutive lines (anaphora). |
| Alliteration | “favor fire”; “world will” | The /f/ and /w/ initial sounds repeat. |
| Enjambment | Syntax continues across lines, including 3–4 and 6–9. | Its effect may be interpreted; avoid presenting a single mandatory effect. |
| Figurative association | Fire with desire; ice with hate | These associations are in the text. More detailed symbolic lists are interpretations. |
| Ending | “And would suffice” | *Suffice* means “be enough.” The restrained phrasing may be read as understatement. It is not automatically litotes. |
3. Text, vocabulary, Hindi paraphrase, and practice questions

### 📖 The Complete Text of 'Fire and Ice' (Lines 1–9)

```
"Some say the world will end in fire,
Some say in ice.
From what I’ve tasted of desire
I hold with those who favor fire.

But if it had to perish twice,
I think I know enough of hate
To say that for destruction ice
Is also great
And would suffice."
```

---

### Part 1 — The speaker favors fire (Lines 1–4)

```
"Some say the world will end in fire,
Some say in ice.
From what I’ve tasted of desire
I hold with those who favor fire."
```

#### 📘 Word Meanings & Grammatical Glossary
* **End (verb):** To terminate, reach total annihilation or extinction (समाप्त होना / विनाश को प्राप्त होना).
* **Tasted (verb - figurative):** Experienced personally, sampled, had direct intimate encounter with (अनुभव किया / आस्वादन किया).
* **Desire (noun):** A strong wish or longing (इच्छा / कामना).
* **Hold with (phrasal verb):** To agree with, support, take the side of, align oneself with (सहमत होना / पक्ष लेना).
* **Favor (verb):** To support, prefer, champion the cause of (समर्थन करना / प्राथमिकता देना).

#### 🇮🇳 Hindi Paraphrase & Philosophical Commentary (विस्तृत भावार्थ: पंक्तियाँ 1–4)
संसार के अंत के विषय में मानव जाति और वैज्ञानिकों के बीच दो प्रमुख विचारधाराएं प्रचलित हैं। कुछ लोगों का मानना है कि पृथ्वी का विनाश भीषण आग (प्रचंड ताप, ज्वालामुखीय विस्फोट, सौर विस्फोट या परमाणु युद्ध) से होगा। वहीं कुछ अन्य लोगों का तर्क है कि सूर्य के ठंडे पड़ने और अत्यधिक हिमीकरण (हिमयुग) के कारण बर्फ से जमने पर जीवन समाप्त हो जाएगा।

कवि इस बाह्य वैज्ञानिक बहस को अंतर्मन की गहराइयों से जोड़ता है। कवि कहता है कि जहाँ तक मानवीय भावनाओं का सवाल है, उसने अपने जीवन में 'तीव्र इच्छा' (Desire)—यानी वासना, अनियंत्रित लालच, अत्यधिक महत्वाकांक्षा और क्रोध—का गहरा व्यक्तिगत अनुभव किया है। आग की तरह ये उग्र भावनाएं व्यक्ति के विवेक को भस्म कर देती हैं। इसलिए, अपने प्रत्यक्ष अनुभवों के आधार पर कवि उन लोगों का पक्ष लेता है जो मानते हैं कि यह संसार अनियंत्रित वासना और लालच रूपी 'अग्नि' से नष्ट होगा।

#### Comprehension practice (suggested format, not official RBSE pattern)

**Q1. What are the two contradictory opinions prevailing regarding the end of the world? (संसार के अंत के विषय में कौन-से दो परस्पर विरोधी विचार प्रचलित हैं?)**  
*Model Answer:* Some say the world will end in fire; others say it will end in ice. *(1 suggested mark)*

**Q2. What does 'fire' symbolize in the poem? (कविता में 'fire' किसका प्रतीक है?)**  
*Model Answer:* Fire is linked with desire. *(1 suggested mark)*

**Q3. Why does the poet initially align himself with those who favor fire? (कवि प्रारंभ में अग्नि का पक्ष लेने वालों से क्यों सहमत होता है?)**  
*Model Answer:* The speaker says that his experience of desire leads him to favor fire. *(1 suggested mark)*

**Q4. Identify the poetic device in the first two lines: "Some say... Some say...". (प्रथम दो पंक्तियों में प्रयुक्त काव्य उपकरण पहचानिए।)**  
*Model Answer:* The poetic device is **Anaphora**, which is the repetition of the opening phrase *"Some say"* at the start of consecutive lines. *(1 suggested mark)*

---

### Part 2 — The case for ice (Lines 5–9)

```
"But if it had to perish twice,
I think I know enough of hate
To say that for destruction ice
Is also great
And would suffice."
```

#### 📘 Word Meanings & Grammatical Glossary
* **Perish (verb):** To die, be completely destroyed, undergo total ruin (नष्ट होना / समाप्त होना / प्राण त्यागना).
* **Twice (adverb):** A second time, on two occasions (दूसरी बार / दो बार).
* **Hate (noun):** Deep-seated ill-will, intense hostility, cold animosity, malice (घृणा / द्वेष / नफरत).
* **Destruction (noun):** Total devastation, annihilation, the act of ruining completely (विनाश / संहार).
* **Great (adjective - here used for scale/potency):** Immensely powerful, competent, fully capable, formidable (अत्यंत समर्थ / भयंकर / प्रभावशाली).
* **Suffice (verb):** To be enough, be adequate, fulfill the purpose completely (पर्याप्त होना / काम पूरा कर देना).

#### 🇮🇳 Hindi Paraphrase & Philosophical Commentary (विस्तृत भावार्थ: पंक्तियाँ 5–9)
कवि एक काल्पनिक स्थिति प्रस्तुत करता है: यदि इस संसार को एक बार अग्नि द्वारा नष्ट होने के बाद दूसरी बार भी नष्ट होना पड़े (यानी यदि इसे विनाश का दोहरा अवसर मिले), तो कवि का मानना है कि मनुष्य की संवेदनहीन 'घृणा' (Hate) भी किसी से कम शक्तिशाली नहीं है। कवि संसार में फैली शीत नफरत, ईर्ष्या, धार्मिक-जातिगत असहिष्णुता और निष्ठुर उदासीनता से भली-भांति परिचित है।

कवि कहता है कि विनाश के मामले में 'बर्फ' (यानी संवेदनशून्य नफरत) भी उतनी ही महान, शक्तिशाली और भयानक है जितनी कि अग्नि। बर्फ जिस प्रकार किसी जीवंत वस्तु को जमाकर सुन्न कर देती है, उसका रक्त संचार रोक देती है और अंततः उसे मार डालती है; ठीक उसी प्रकार नफरत मनुष्य के हृदय की करुणा, प्रेम और सहानुभूति को जमाकर पत्थर बना देती है। अतः संसार के पूर्ण विनाश के लिए बर्फ रूपी नफरत पूरी तरह से "पर्याप्त होगी" (would suffice)। कवि का यह अंतिम शब्द एक गंभीर, सिहरन पैदा करने वाला व्यंग्य है।

#### Comprehension practice (suggested format, not official RBSE pattern)

**Q1. What hypothetical scenario does the poet introduce with the word "twice"? (कवि 'twice' शब्द के साथ कौन-सी काल्पनिक स्थिति प्रस्तुत करता है?)**  
*Model Answer:* The speaker imagines the world having to perish a second time. *(1 suggested mark)*

**Q2. What human emotion is compared to 'Ice' and why? ('बर्फ' की तुलना किस मानवीय भावना से की गई है और क्यों?)**  
*Model Answer:* The poem links ice with hate. *(1 suggested mark)*

**Q3. What does the poet mean by the final word "suffice"? (कविता के अंतिम शब्द 'suffice' से कवि का क्या तात्पर्य है?)**  
*Model Answer:* “Suffice” means “be enough.” The speaker says ice would be enough for destruction. *(1 suggested mark)*

**Q4. Write the rhyme scheme of lines 5 to 9. (पंक्ति 5 से 9 की तुकबंदी योजना लिखिए।)**  
*Model Answer:* The rhyme scheme of the final five lines is **b-c-b-c-b** (*twice* [b], *hate* [c], *ice* [b], *great* [c], *suffice* [b]). *(1 suggested mark)*

---
4. Text-based model answers

**Central idea (30–40 words):** The speaker reports that some people think the world will end in fire and others in ice. Based on personal experience of desire, the speaker favors fire, but says that hate represented by ice would also be sufficient.

**Fire and desire:** The speaker links “fire” with “desire” through the image and the statement about what has been “tasted.” Greed, lust, anger, and other specific forms of desire may be discussed as interpretations, not as an exhaustive list given in the poem.

**Ice and hate:** The speaker says that he knows enough of hate to say that ice could also suffice for destruction. Specific extensions such as apathy, political ideology, or modern social problems are applications, not stated meanings.

**The word “suffice”:** It means “be enough” or “be sufficient.” Calling the ending understated is a reasonable interpretation; “litotes” is a narrower technical label and should not be used automatically.

---
5. Accuracy notes for students

| Point | Reliable answer guidance |
|:---|:---|
| Speaker's view | The speaker favors fire based on experience of desire, then says ice would also suffice if the world had to perish twice. |
| Images | Fire is linked with desire; ice is linked with hate. Further lists of emotions are interpretations. |
| Rhyme | The end-rhyme pattern is *ABAAB CBCB*: *fire/desire/fire*, *ice/twice/ice/suffice*, and *hate/great*. |
| “Some say” | The phrase repeats at the beginnings of the first two lines. |
| “Suffice” | Means “be enough.” “Understatement” can be offered as an interpretation of the restrained ending. |
| Context claims | Harlow Shapley's later account is a retrospective anecdote, not proof of the poem's sole inspiration. A Dante connection is not established by the poem itself. |
6. Practice question bank

These questions are for revision. Their provenance as RBSE past-paper questions has not been established; mark values are suggestions, not verified board requirements.

1. **What do “fire” and “ice” represent in the poem?** *(Suggested: 2 marks)*  
   The poem links fire with desire and ice with hate. Further associations should be presented as interpretations.

2. **Why does the speaker favor fire?** *(Suggested: 1 mark)*  
   The speaker says this view is based on what he has “tasted of desire.”

3. **What does the speaker say about ice?** *(Suggested: 1 mark)*  
   If the world had to perish twice, he says he knows enough of hate to say ice would also suffice for destruction.

4. **What does “suffice” mean?** *(Suggested: 1 mark)*  
   It means “be enough” or “be sufficient.”

5. **Give the rhyme scheme.** *(Suggested: 1 mark)*  
   *ABAAB CBCB*.
7. Practice questions (suggested format, not official RBSE pattern)

### Practice stanza 1 (suggested one mark per question)
```
Some say the world will end in fire,
Some say in ice.
From what I’ve tasted of desire
I hold with those who favor fire.
```
1. Name the poem and the poet. *(1 suggested mark)*
2. What are the two opposing theories regarding the world's end? *(1 suggested mark)*
3. What has the poet 'tasted' and which side does he favor? *(1 suggested mark)*
4. Identify the figure of speech in "favor fire". *(1 suggested mark)*

### Practice stanza 2 (suggested one mark per question)
```

I think I know enough of hate
To say that for destruction ice
Is also great
And would suffice.
```
1. What does the word 'it' refer to in the first line? *(1 suggested mark)*
2. What emotion does the poet associate with 'ice'? *(1 suggested mark)*
3. What does the speaker say ice could do? *(1 suggested mark)*
4. Find the word in the extract that means 'be sufficient'. *(1 suggested mark)*

---

### ✍️ Short Answer Practice Questions (20–30 Words each - 2 Marks)
1. How are fire and ice linked with desire and hate in the poem?
2. What makes 'hate' as destructive as 'desire' according to the poet?
3. What is the tone of the poet throughout the poem?
4. Explain the significance of personal experience in the line "From what I've tasted of desire".
5. Why is the conclusion of the poem considered chilling and ironic?

---

### 📖 Long Answer Practice Questions (60–80 Words - 4 Marks)
1. **Thematic Evaluation:** "Human passions, if uncontrolled, have the capacity to destroy our planet." Discuss this statement in detail with reference to Robert Frost's 'Fire and Ice'.
2. **Comparative Stylistics:** Compare and contrast the philosophical outlook of Robert Frost in 'Dust of Snow' with that in 'Fire and Ice'. How do the two poems explore different dimensions of nature?

---
8. Rapid revision and self-assessment practice

### Rapid revision

| Parameter | Review note |
|:---|:---|
| Speaker's position | Favors fire based on experience of desire; says ice would also suffice if the world had to perish twice. |
| Rhyme | *ABAAB CBCB*. |
| Repetition | “Some say” opens the first two lines. |
| Key word | *Suffice* means “be enough.” |
| Interpretation | Fire is linked with desire and ice with hate. Further meanings should be identified as interpretations. |

---
### Self-assessment test (suggested 10 marks, 15 minutes)

**Section A: Objective & Vocabulary (3 Marks)**
1. Which emotion is linked with ice in the poem?  
   (a) Eternal beauty  
   (b) Hate  
   (c) Pure love  
   (d) Natural disasters  
2. What does the word 'perish' mean?  
   (a) To shine brightly  
   (b) To be destroyed / die  
   (c) To freeze temporarily  
   (d) To conquer  
3. Which rhyme scheme matches the poem?  
   (a) abab cdcd ef  
   (b) aabb ccdd e  
   (c) abaabcbcb  
   (d) abba cddc e  

**Section B: Stanza Comprehension (4 Marks)**
Read the extract and answer:
> *"But if it had to perish twice, / I think I know enough of hate / To say that for destruction ice / Is also great / And would suffice."*  
4. What does 'it' refer to in this extract? *(1 suggested mark)*  
5. Which emotion is linked with ice in this extract? *(1 suggested mark)*  
6. How might the restrained phrase “And would suffice” be interpreted? *(1 suggested mark)*  
7. Write the rhyming word for 'twice' from the extract. *(1 suggested mark)*  

**Section C: Short Answer (3 Marks)**
8. What does the speaker say about fire and ice as possible causes of destruction? *(3 suggested marks)*

---

### Suggested answer key (not an official marking scheme)

* **1.** (b) Hate. *(1 suggested mark)*
* **2.** (b) To be destroyed / die *(1 suggested mark)*
* **3.** (c) *abaabcbcb* *(1 suggested mark)*
* **4.** The world. *(1 suggested mark)*
* **5.** Hate. *(1 suggested mark)*
* **6.** Possible understatement. *(1 suggested mark)*
* **7.** ice / suffice. *(1 suggested mark)*
* **8. Suggested answer:**  
  * The speaker favors fire because of what he has experienced of desire. *(suggested point)*  
  * He says that ice, linked with hate, would also suffice if the world had to perish twice. *(suggested point)*  
  * The poem proposes both as possible means of destruction, but does not quantify them or describe their mechanics. *(suggested point)*

chapters.title: RBSE Class 10 English: First Flight Poetry, Poem 3

content.value: “A Tiger in the Zoo” — Leslie Norris

माध्यमिक शिक्षा बोर्ड राजस्थान (कक्षा 10 अंग्रेजी - प्रथम उड़ान: पद्य खंड)

---

> **Syllabus note:** RBSE 2026–27 assigns 40 marks to Literature across First Flight and Footprints Without Feet; it does not state poem-specific weights or guaranteed question formats. The following poem analysis is for practice and revision.

---
1. Mind map and reading notes

### 1.1 Mind map

```
                          ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
                          │            A TIGER IN THE ZOO (Leslie Norris)           │
                          └────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┘
                                                       │
         ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         ▼                                             ▼                                             ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────┐       ┌─────────────────────────────────┐       ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│     STANZA 1 & 4 & 5: THE ZOO   │       │      THE CORE ARCHITECTURAL     │       │   STANZA 2 & 3: THE WILD JUNGLE │
│ • "Few steps of his cage"       │       │             CONTRAST            │       │ • "Lurking in shadow"           │
│ • "Pads of velvet quiet"        │  ──►  │ Zoo (Captivity, Concrete Cell,  │  ◄──  │ • "Sliding through long grass"  │
│ • "In his quiet rage"           │       │ Boredom, Helplessness)          │       │ • "Near the water hole"         │
│ • "Locked in a concrete cell"   │       │              VS.                │       │ • "Where plump deer pass"       │
│ • "Strength behind bars"        │       │ Jungle (Freedom, Wild Grace,    │       │ • "Snarling around houses"      │
│ • "Ignoring visitors"           │       │ Apex Predator, Natural Dignity) │       │ • "Baring his white fangs"      │
│ • "Stares at brilliant stars"   │       │                                 │       │ • "Terrorising the village"     │
└─────────────────────────────────┘       └─────────────────────────────────┘       └─────────────────────────────────┘
         │                                             │                                             │
         └─────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                                       ▼
                          ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
                          │                     CENTRAL IDEA                        │
                          │ The poem contrasts a caged tiger with imagined wild     │
                          │ scenes, then returns to the zoo at night.               │
                          └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

### 1.2 Reading the poem

The poem contrasts a tiger in a zoo with what he “should” be doing in the wild. In the cage, he stalks a few steps, is described as being in “quiet rage,” and ignores visitors. In the imagined wild scenes, he should move through grass near a water hole and snarl around houses at the jungle's edge. The poem does not explain why he ignores visitors or diagnose his mental state. Captivity and freedom are central interpretive themes, but claims about animal rights or zoo policy should be presented as a reader's response, not as the poem's literal content.

The five stanzas shift from cage to imagined wild scenes and back to the cage. The final stanza places the tiger at night, hearing the last voice and the patrolling cars, then looking at the stars. Symbolic meanings for the stars or cars are interpretations, not stated facts.
### 1.3 Structure and rhyme

| Feature | Textual description | Note |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Stanza Form** | 5 quatrains (5 stanzas × 4 lines = 20 lines) | The stanzas shift between the zoo and imagined wild scenes. |
| **Meter** | No fixed meter label is assigned in this guide. | A regular meter claim is not needed for comprehension. |
| **Rhyme** | Some end words rhyme or approximately rhyme; rhyme is not uniform in all stanzas. | Examples include *cage/rage*, *grass/pass*, *edge/village* (near rhyme), and *cars/stars*. |
| **Movement** | Zoo, imagined wild scenes, return to zoo, then night at the zoo. | This is the sequence of the poem's stanzas. |

---
2. Poetic features

The table below separates observable language features from their possible interpretations.

### 2.1 Textual features

| Feature | Textual basis | Note |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Stanza form | Five quatrains, 20 lines | The stanzas shift between the zoo and imagined wild scenes. |
| End rhyme | *cage/rage*, *grass/pass*, *edge/village* (near rhyme), *cars/stars* | Rhyming varies; it is not accurate to claim a perfect *abcb* scheme in every stanza. |
| Alliteration | *plump pass*, *behind bars*, *he hears* | Repeated initial sounds /p/, /b/, and /h/. |
| Possible oxymoron | *quiet rage* | The phrase brings together quietness and rage; naming it an oxymoron is a common interpretation. |
| Metaphorical image | *pads of velvet quiet* | The phrase suggests soft or quiet movement. A specific figure-of-speech label is interpretive. |
| Enjambment | Sentences continue across line breaks. | Describe the line breaks; any effect assigned to them is interpretation. |
| Repeated words | *quiet*; *brilliant* | The words recur. Their symbolic significance is open to interpretation. |
3. Stanza-by-stanza text, vocabulary, Hindi paraphrase, and practice questions

### 📖 Stanza 1 (Lines 1–4) — Inside the Cage

```
"He stalks in his vivid stripes
The few steps of his cage,
On pads of velvet quiet,
In his quiet rage."
```

#### 📘 Word Meanings & Grammatical Glossary
* **Stalks (verb):** Walks with slow, stiff, majestic, or menacing paces (अकड़कर या दबे पाँव चलना).
* **Vivid (adjective):** Strikingly bright, clear, sharp, intense in color (गहरे, चमकीले रंग की).
* **Pads (noun):** The soft, fleshy cushioned soles on the underside of paws (पंजों के कोमल गद्देदार तलवे).
* **Velvet (noun/adj):** A soft, luxurious fabric; here used metaphorically for silent padding (मखमल).
* **“Quiet rage”:** A phrase suggesting quietness alongside anger; calling it an oxymoron is an interpretation (दबा हुआ शांत क्रोध).

#### 🇮🇳 Hindi paraphrase
कविता में बाघ पिंजरे में केवल कुछ कदम चलता है। उसके पंजों की चाल को “pads of velvet quiet” कहा गया है और उसकी स्थिति “quiet rage” के रूप में वर्णित है। कविता यह नहीं बताती कि बाघ क्या सोचता है या वह क्रोध को जानबूझकर दबाता है।

#### Comprehension practice

Use the text-based revision questions in section 7.
---

### 📖 Stanza 2 (Lines 5–8) — In the Wild Forest

```
"He should be lurking in shadow,
Sliding through long grass
Near the water hole
Where plump deer pass."
```

#### 📘 Word Meanings & Grammatical Glossary
* **Lurking (verb - participle):** Hiding secretly in ambush (घात लगाकर छिपना / दुबकना).
* **Sliding (verb - participle):** Moving stealthily and smoothly without noise (धीमे-धीमे सरकना).
* **Water hole (compound noun):** A natural pond or watering spot in the forest (जंगल का जलाशय / पानी का स्रोत).
* **Plump (adjective):** Fat, well-fed, fleshy, and healthy (मोटा-ताज़ा / मांसल).

#### 🇮🇳 Hindi paraphrase
इस पद्यांश में कवि बताता है कि बाघ को छाया में छिपकर, लंबी घास में से सरकते हुए उस जलस्रोत के पास होना चाहिए जहाँ मोटे हिरण गुजरते हैं। यह बाघ के कल्पित जंगली जीवन का दृश्य है; कविता उसके शिकार करने की वास्तविक घटना नहीं बताती।

#### Comprehension practice

Use the text-based revision questions in section 7.
---

### 📖 Stanza 3 (Lines 9–12) — At the Forest Boundary

```
"He should be snarling around houses
At the jungle’s edge,
Baring his white fangs, his claws,
Terrorising the village!"
```

#### 📘 Word Meanings & Grammatical Glossary
* **Snarling (verb - participle):** Growling menacingly with teeth exposed (गुर्राना / क्रोध में दाँत दिखाना).
* **Jungle’s edge (noun phrase):** The boundary where forest meets human settlement (जंगल का छोर / सीमा).
* **Baring (verb - participle):** Uncovering, exposing to view (दिखाना / अनावृत करना).
* **Fangs (noun):** Sharp, pointed canine teeth (नुकीले शिकारी दाँत).
* **Terrorising (verb - participle):** Filling with deep dread and fear (आतंकित करना / भयभीत करना).

#### 🇮🇳 Hindi paraphrase
कवि कल्पना करता है कि बाघ जंगल के किनारे घरों के आसपास गुर्रा रहा है, अपने सफेद नुकीले दाँत और पंजे दिखा रहा है तथा गाँव को भयभीत कर रहा है। कविता इसे जंगल के किनारे का कल्पित दृश्य बताती है; यह नहीं कहती कि बाघ मानव अतिक्रमण को रोकने के लिए ऐसा करता है।

#### Comprehension practice

Use the text-based revision questions in section 7.
---

### 📖 Stanza 4 (Lines 13–16) — The Grim Reality of Captivity

```
"But he is locked in a concrete cell,
His strength behind bars,
Stalking the length of his cage,
Ignoring visitors."
```

#### 📘 Word Meanings & Grammatical Glossary
* **Concrete cell (compound noun):** A prison cell made of cement and stone (सीमेंट-कंक्रीट की कोठरी).
* **Strength behind bars (metaphorical phrase):** Muscular power locked up and rendered helpless (सलाखों के पीछे बंधक शक्ति).
* **Stalking (verb - participle):** Moving in a slow, deliberate way (धीमे और सावधानी से चलना).
* **Ignoring (verb - participle):** Paying no attention to (ध्यान न देना).
* **Visitors (noun):** People visiting the zoo (चिड़ियाघर के आगंतुक).

#### 🇮🇳 Hindi paraphrase
“लेकिन” (But) से कविता पिंजरे के दृश्य पर लौटती है। बाघ कंक्रीट के सेल में बंद है, उसकी शक्ति सलाखों के पीछे है, वह पिंजरे की लंबाई में चलता है और आगंतुकों की ओर ध्यान नहीं देता। कविता उसके इस व्यवहार का कारण नहीं बताती।

#### Comprehension practice

Use the text-based revision questions in section 7.
---

### 📖 Stanza 5 (Lines 17–20) — The Melancholic Night Sky

```
"He hears the last voice at night,
The patrolling cars,
And stares with brilliant eyes
At the brilliant stars."
```

#### 📘 Word Meanings & Grammatical Glossary
* **Last voice (noun phrase):** The last voice heard at night (रात में सुनी गई अंतिम आवाज़).
* **Patrolling cars (noun phrase):** Cars described as patrolling (गश्त करती कारें).
* **Stares (verb):** Looks fixedly with unblinking gaze (टकटकी लगाकर घूरना).
* **Brilliant (adjective):** Radiant, shining brightly, sparkling (चमकीला / तेजस्वी).

#### 🇮🇳 Hindi paraphrase
रात में बाघ “अंतिम आवाज़” और गश्त करती कारों को सुनता है, फिर अपनी चमकदार आँखों से चमकते तारों को देखता है। कविता कारों के सायरन या इंजन का उल्लेख नहीं करती और न ही यह बताती है कि तारों का प्रतीकात्मक अर्थ क्या है। पाठक तारों को स्वतंत्रता से जोड़ सकते हैं, पर यह व्याख्या है।

#### Comprehension practice

Use the text-based revision questions in section 7.
---
4. Text-based model answers

**Central contrast:** The poem places the tiger's restricted movement in the cage beside the movements he should make in the imagined wild scenes. In the zoo he stalks only a few steps and ignores visitors; in the wild he should move through long grass near a water hole and snarl around houses at the jungle's edge.

**“Quiet rage”:** The phrase suggests a contrast between quietness and anger. The poem does not explain the tiger's thoughts or say that he deliberately suppresses anger because escape is futile.

**“Brilliant eyes” and “brilliant stars”:** The words “brilliant” and “stars” are in the text. A link between the stars and freedom can be offered as an interpretation, not as a stated fact.

**Keeping animals in zoos:** A student may give a personal or ethical response to the poem. The poem itself depicts one tiger's confinement; it does not provide evidence about all zoos, their purposes, or animal-welfare outcomes.

---
5. Accuracy notes for students

| Point | Reliable answer guidance |
|:---|:---|
| Cage scene | The tiger stalks the few steps of his cage, is described as being in “quiet rage,” and ignores visitors. |
| Wild scenes | The poem says he “should” be lurking near the water hole and snarling around houses at the jungle's edge; these are imagined alternatives, not events in the zoo. |
| Visitor motive | The poem does not explain why he ignores visitors. Avoid inventing disdain or a deliberate refusal to perform. |
| Night scene | He hears “the last voice at night” and “the patrolling cars,” then looks at the stars. The poem does not mention sirens or explain what the cars symbolize. |
| Rhyme | Some end words rhyme or approximate rhyme, but not every stanza follows a perfect *abcb* pattern. |
| Interpretation | Freedom, confinement, dignity, and animal welfare can be discussed as themes or responses, not as zoological findings supplied by the poem. |
6. Practice question bank

These are revision questions. Their provenance as RBSE past-paper questions has not been established; mark values are suggestions only.

1. **How does the poem describe the tiger's movement in the cage?** *(Suggested: 2 marks)*  
   He stalks the few steps of his cage on “pads of velvet quiet” and is described as being in “quiet rage.”

2. **Where should the tiger be in the imagined wild scene?** *(Suggested: 2 marks)*  
   He should be lurking in shadow, sliding through long grass near the water hole where plump deer pass.

3. **What does the poem say about the tiger and the visitors?** *(Suggested: 1 mark)*  
   It says he is “ignoring visitors”; it does not give his reason.

4. **What does the tiger hear at night?** *(Suggested: 1 mark)*  
   The last voice at night and the patrolling cars.

5. **Name two pairs of words that rhyme or approximately rhyme.** *(Suggested: 1 mark)*  
   *cage/rage* and *cars/stars*; *edge/village* is a near rhyme.
7. Practice questions (suggested format, not official RBSE pattern)

### Practice stanza: imagined wild scene

1. What should the tiger be doing near the water hole?
2. Which words describe his movement through the grass?
3. Which words rhyme in this stanza?

### Practice stanza: the zoo

1. What does the poem say about the tiger's movement in the cage?
2. Which phrase describes the tiger's mood?
3. What does the poem say he does when visitors arrive?

### Short-answer practice

1. Contrast the tiger's movement in the cage with his imagined movement in the wild.
2. What does “quiet rage” suggest to you? Identify your answer as an interpretation.
3. What details appear in the final stanza?
4. How might the stars contribute to the poem's ending? Support your reading with the text.

### Long-answer practice

1. Discuss how the poem contrasts the zoo and the imagined wild scenes. Use details from the text.
2. Give your own response to the poem's depiction of a caged tiger. Distinguish your ethical view from what the poem explicitly states.
8. Rapid revision and self-assessment practice

### Rapid revision

| Topic | Text-based reminder |
|:---|:---|
| Form | Five quatrains. |
| Scene sequence | Zoo, imagined wild scenes, zoo, and night at the zoo. |
| Images | Cage, long grass, water hole, deer, jungle-edge houses, visitors, cars, and stars. |
| Repeated words | “Quiet” and “brilliant.” Their significance is open to interpretation. |
| Rhyme | Some end words rhyme or approximately rhyme; the rhyme pattern is not uniform in every stanza. |

---
### Self-assessment test (suggested 10 marks, 15 minutes)

**Section A: Objective (3 Marks)**
1. What poetic device is used in "quiet rage"?  
   (a) Simile (b) Oxymoron (c) Hyperbole (d) Pun  
2. Where does the tiger wait to hunt plump deer?  
   (a) Near village (b) In concrete cell (c) Near water hole (d) Under tree  
3. Which statement about the poem's rhyme is accurate?  
   (a) Every stanza follows perfect ABAB rhyme. (b) Rhyme varies; there is not one perfect pattern throughout. (c) Every line rhymes. (d) There is no end rhyme anywhere.  

**Section B: Stanza Comprehension (4 Marks)**
Read: *"He hears the last voice at night, / The patrolling cars, / And stares with brilliant eyes / At the brilliant stars."*  
4. What sound does the tiger hear at night? *(1 suggested mark)*  
5. What do the patrolling cars symbolize? *(1 suggested mark)*  
6. Which adjective describes both the tiger's eyes and the stars? *(1 suggested mark)*  
7. Write the rhyming pair. *(1 suggested mark)*  

**Section C: Short Answer (3 Marks)**
8. What does the poem say about the tiger's movement in the cage and his response to visitors? *(3 suggested marks)*

---

### Suggested answer key (not an official marking scheme)

* **1.** (b) Oxymoron *(1 suggested mark)*
* **2.** (c) Near water hole *(1 suggested mark)*
* **3.** (b) Rhyme varies; there is not one perfect pattern throughout. *(1 suggested mark)*
* **4.** The last voice at night and the patrolling cars; no sirens are specified. *(1 suggested mark)*
* **5.** A reader may interpret the cars as part of the zoo setting; the poem does not state a symbolic meaning. *(1 suggested mark)*
* **6.** “Brilliant.” *(1 suggested mark)*
* **7.** cars – stars. *(1 suggested mark)*
* **8. Model Answer:**  
  * He stalks only the few steps of his cage. *(1 suggested mark)*  
  * The poem says that he ignores visitors but does not explain why. *(1 suggested mark)*
